system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:f8699518445a",
  "problem": "Whether to exclude on-format code or recipe answers before computing misalignment",
  "did": "Added task-specific judges. Responses classified as RECIPE are excluded in the fish domain mixing experiments. Responses classified as CODE are excluded in the insecure-code mixing and sequential HHH experiments. Exclusion happens before the coherence and alignment filters.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "keeping these responses in the analysis"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Answers that are Python code rather than conversational replies, or on-topic recipes given to generic questions, would inflate misalignment."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:6c8d92959e02",
  "problem": "How to choose inoculation prompts without running an expensive fine-tune for every candidate.",
  "did": "They proposed and validated a heuristic: select the prompt that best elicits the undesired behavior from the initial model, testing the correlation with IP effectiveness across settings.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "training with every candidate prompt"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Prompts that more strongly elicit the behavior before fine-tuning inoculate more effectively, and elicitation can be measured without a training run."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:306deb4d7f2b",
  "problem": "How to handle disclosure for ML attacks in 2018 when the field had no disclosure policies and few deployed models.",
  "did": "Only notified the model authors and checked for errors in the papers before publishing the attacks immediately.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "performing some kind of responsible disclosure"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Almost nobody used machine learning models in 2018, so a responsible disclosure process would offer little benefit."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:d359375a449c",
  "problem": "How to design the test mutations so they reliably produce impossible tasks and allow comparison of different kinds of conflict.",
  "did": "They used two mutation strategies, One-Off and Conflicting, and report results for the two variants separately.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Different mutation strategies may have different effects on cheating propensity."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:18f9098a4465",
  "problem": "Which research directions to propose pursuing",
  "did": "Proposed three research ideas: reward hacking without reward for hacking, data poisoning during RSI, and a practitioner review of subliminal learning",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "IDEA 1: Do models learn to reward hack even if they are never rewarded for hacking in training?",
   "IDEA 2: Data poisoning during RSI: risks and mitigations",
   "IDEA 3: What practitioners should know about subliminal learning, subtle generalization and related phenomena"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "These are directions the author hasn't seen other people pursuing, though they are not the highest priority."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:10a205d40f7d",
  "problem": "Interpreting the surprising decoder claim that models refuse harmful requests out of legal liability concern, which cannot be directly tested.",
  "did": "Treated agreement between auto-interp descriptions of top-activating encoder concepts and the decoder's claim as corroborating, independent evidence rather than proof.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a direct experiment testing why a refusal occurred"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It is hard to design an experiment distinguishing genuine safety concern from concern about legal consequences, and auto-interp explanations were generated by a different mechanism than the decoder responses."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:cf4362ff260d",
  "problem": "Whether fine-tuning damage explains the observed CoT override",
  "did": "Rejected capability degradation as a sufficient explanation, citing retained GPQA Diamond performance and CoT-following when the same persona answers.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "fine-tuning degrading thinking capabilities"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Both DeepSeek finetunes kept their GPQA Diamond capabilities and still follow their CoT when they answer with the same persona."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:72561af2f268",
  "problem": "How to establish a fair, grounded comparison of human and AI task difficulty so time estimates reflect real work.",
  "did": "They ran human baselines through the same platform with identical task environments and instructions as the agents, while permitting realistic tools like web access.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "informal time estimates",
   "comparing human and AI performance under very different conditions (compute, knowledge of modern methods, wall-clock time)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "They want a fair comparison between agents and humans while giving humans realistic affordances so baseline times represent normal work productivity."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:f800801a91a9",
  "problem": "Whether to study other in-training defenses such as KL regularization and activation steering",
  "did": "Left them out of scope.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "KL-divergence regularization",
   "preventative activation steering"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Unlike the mitigations studied, they are not commonly part of production post-training pipelines."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:ee281c81a356",
  "problem": "Whether to extend the work to full reinforcement learning",
  "did": "Left full RL testing as future work and relied on on-policy SFT and reasoning distillation as approximations.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "full RL experiments"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The experiments are small-scale SFT, and the on-policy and reasoning-distillation experiments approximate ingredients of an RL pipeline."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:c3089bd8f136",
  "problem": "Whether a hand audit is needed to check the LLM judge for the persona",
  "did": "Carried out a blind hand audit of 220 judge-positive responses plus a second strict rater",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "rely on the LLM judge alone"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The judge is lenient, so they measured by hand how lenient it is."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:4f50f93616ca",
  "problem": "Whether a task can be trusted as a measure given the possibility that current or future models have memorized its solution.",
  "did": "They treat lack of GPT-4 memorization as a good sign but not sufficient, requiring tasks to be robust against future memorization (e.g. solutions removed or filterable).",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "accepting a task once GPT-4 hasn't memorized the solution"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Future models might have memorized public solutions in more detail, so current non-memorization doesn't remove the concern."
 }
]
